claim: Activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR) sustains protein homeostasis (proteostasis) and plays a fundamental role in tissue maintenance and longevity of organisms.
source: Activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR) sustains protein homeostasis (proteostasis) and plays a fundamental role in tissue maintenance and longevity of organisms.
evidence: This is a general statement about UPR function that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Long-range control of UPR activation has been demonstrated in invertebrates.
source: Long-range control of UPR activation has been demonstrated in invertebrates, but such mechanisms in mammals remain elusive.
evidence: This statement references established findings in invertebrate biology, supported by citations elsewhere in the manuscript (Sun et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2014; Taylor and Dillin, 2013).

claim: Long-range control mechanisms of UPR activation in mammals remain elusive.
source: Long-range control of UPR activation has been demonstrated in invertebrates, but such mechanisms in mammals remain elusive.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge about mammalian UPR regulation.

claim: The female sex hormone estrogen regulates the UPR in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs).
source: Here, we show that the female sex hormone estrogen regulates the UPR in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental results including RNA-seq, qPCR, and functional assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Estrogen treatment increases the capacity of HSCs to regenerate the hematopoietic system upon transplantation.
source: Estrogen treatment increases the capacity of HSCs to regenerate the hematopoietic system upon transplantation and accelerates regeneration after irradiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation experiments shown in Figure 1E-J demonstrating enhanced multilineage reconstitution.

claim: Estrogen treatment accelerates hematopoietic regeneration after irradiation.
source: Estrogen treatment increases the capacity of HSCs to regenerate the hematopoietic system upon transplantation and accelerates regeneration after irradiation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2A-C showing accelerated recovery of peripheral blood cells after total body irradiation.

claim: Estrogen signals through estrogen receptor α (ERα) expressed in hematopoietic cells to activate the protective Ire1α-Xbp1 branch of the UPR.
source: We found that estrogen signals through estrogen receptor α (ERα) expressed in hematopoietic cells to activate the protective Ire1α-Xbp1 branch of the UPR.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using ERα-deficient mice (Figure 1, Figure 4) showing loss of E2 effects and UPR activation.

claim: ERα-mediated activation of the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway confers HSCs with resistance against proteotoxic stress.
source: Further, ERα-mediated activation of the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway confers HSCs with resistance against proteotoxic stress and promotes regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing reduced apoptosis and improved colony formation in E2-treated cells exposed to ER stressors (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: ERα-mediated activation of the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway promotes hematopoietic regeneration.
source: Further, ERα-mediated activation of the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway confers HSCs with resistance against proteotoxic stress and promotes regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR deletion experiments showing that Ire1α is required for E2-mediated enhancement of hematopoietic recovery (Figure 6E-G).

claim: Stem cells in the intestine, central nervous system, hematopoietic system, and germline are regulated by insulin and nutritional status.
source: For instance, stem cells in the intestine, central nervous system, hematopoietic system, and germline are regulated by insulin and nutritional status (Chell and Brand, 2010; Cheng et al., 2014; LaFever and Drummond-Barbosa, 2005; Lehtinen et al., 2011; McLeod et al., 2010; O'Brien et al., 2011; Sousa-Nunes et al., 2011; Yilmaz et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: The circadian rhythm affects skin and hematopoietic stem cells.
source: and the circadian rhythm affects skin and hematopoietic stem cells (Janich et al., 2011; Méndez-Ferrer et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Age-related changes in blood-borne factors regulate muscle and neural stem cell aging.
source: Age-related changes in blood-borne factors regulate muscle and neural stem cell aging (Brack et al., 2007; Conboy et al., 2005; Katsimpardi et al., 2014; Sinha et al., 2014; Villeda et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Prostaglandin E2 is a long-range signal that augments the ability of tissue stem cells to repair damaged tissues.
source: However, few long-range signals, such as prostaglandin E2 (North et al., 2007) or those that are modulated by prolonged fasting (Cheng et al., 2014), have been found to augment the ability of tissue stem cells to repair damaged tissues.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Signals modulated by prolonged fasting augment the ability of tissue stem cells to repair damaged tissues.
source: However, few long-range signals, such as prostaglandin E2 (North et al., 2007) or those that are modulated by prolonged fasting (Cheng et al., 2014), have been found to augment the ability of tissue stem cells to repair damaged tissues.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: A single hematopoietic stem cell can rebuild the entire hematopoietic system upon transplantation.
source: The hematopoietic system has a remarkable regenerative potential demonstrated by the ability of a single hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) to rebuild the entire hematopoietic system upon transplantation, and to regenerate the tissue upon damage, such as those caused by chemo- or radio-therapies.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of hematopoietic stem cell biology.

claim: HSCs can regenerate the hematopoietic tissue upon damage caused by chemo- or radio-therapies.
source: The hematopoietic system has a remarkable regenerative potential demonstrated by the ability of a single hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) to rebuild the entire hematopoietic system upon transplantation, and to regenerate the tissue upon damage, such as those caused by chemo- or radio-therapies.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of hematopoietic stem cell biology.

claim: Stem cell factor is a cell-extrinsic factor produced by the HSC niche that promotes regeneration by HSCs.
source: Cell-extrinsic factors produced by the HSC niche, such as the stem cell factor (Zsebo et al., 1992), angiogenin (Goncalves et al., 2016), pleiotrophin (Himburg et al., 2010), EGF (Doan et al., 2013), or Dkk1 (Himburg et al., 2017) have particular therapeutic potential as they may be used as radioprotectors or radiomitigators to accelerate the recovery of the hematopoietic system (Citrin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Angiogenin is a cell-extrinsic factor produced by the HSC niche that promotes regeneration by HSCs.
source: Cell-extrinsic factors produced by the HSC niche, such as the stem cell factor (Zsebo et al., 1992), angiogenin (Goncalves et al., 2016), pleiotrophin (Himburg et al., 2010), EGF (Doan et al., 2013), or Dkk1 (Himburg et al., 2017) have particular therapeutic potential as they may be used as radioprotectors or radiomitigators to accelerate the recovery of the hematopoietic system (Citrin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Pleiotrophin is a cell-extrinsic factor produced by the HSC niche that promotes regeneration by HSCs.
source: Cell-extrinsic factors produced by the HSC niche, such as the stem cell factor (Zsebo et al., 1992), angiogenin (Goncalves et al., 2016), pleiotrophin (Himburg et al., 2010), EGF (Doan et al., 2013), or Dkk1 (Himburg et al., 2017) have particular therapeutic potential as they may be used as radioprotectors or radiomitigators to accelerate the recovery of the hematopoietic system (Citrin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: EGF is a cell-extrinsic factor produced by the HSC niche that promotes regeneration by HSCs.
source: Cell-extrinsic factors produced by the HSC niche, such as the stem cell factor (Zsebo et al., 1992), angiogenin (Goncalves et al., 2016), pleiotrophin (Himburg et al., 2010), EGF (Doan et al., 2013), or Dkk1 (Himburg et al., 2017) have particular therapeutic potential as they may be used as radioprotectors or radiomitigators to accelerate the recovery of the hematopoietic system (Citrin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Dkk1 is a cell-extrinsic factor produced by the HSC niche that promotes regeneration by HSCs.
source: Cell-extrinsic factors produced by the HSC niche, such as the stem cell factor (Zsebo et al., 1992), angiogenin (Goncalves et al., 2016), pleiotrophin (Himburg et al., 2010), EGF (Doan et al., 2013), or Dkk1 (Himburg et al., 2017) have particular therapeutic potential as they may be used as radioprotectors or radiomitigators to accelerate the recovery of the hematopoietic system (Citrin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Niche-derived factors have therapeutic potential as radioprotectors or radiomitigators to accelerate hematopoietic system recovery.
source: Cell-extrinsic factors produced by the HSC niche, such as the stem cell factor (Zsebo et al., 1992), angiogenin (Goncalves et al., 2016), pleiotrophin (Himburg et al., 2010), EGF (Doan et al., 2013), or Dkk1 (Himburg et al., 2017) have particular therapeutic potential as they may be used as radioprotectors or radiomitigators to accelerate the recovery of the hematopoietic system (Citrin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Maternal E2 stored in the yolk promotes the specification of HSCs during zebrafish development.
source: During zebrafish development, maternal E2 stored in the yolk promotes the specification of HSCs (Carroll et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: E2 produced by the ovaries stimulates division of HSCs via the estrogen receptor α (ERα) in mice.
source: In mice, E2 produced by the ovaries stimulates division of HSCs via the estrogen receptor α (ERα).
evidence: This statement references findings from the authors' previous work (Nakada et al., 2014).

claim: Exogenous E2, when administered at a physiological level similar to pregnancy, promotes division of HSCs in male mice.
source: Exogenous E2, when administered at a physiological level similar to the level observed during pregnancy, also promotes division of HSCs in male mice, indicating that the E2-ERα pathway activation is sufficient induce HSC division (Nakada et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The E2-ERα pathway activation is sufficient to induce HSC division.
source: Exogenous E2, when administered at a physiological level similar to the level observed during pregnancy, also promotes division of HSCs in male mice, indicating that the E2-ERα pathway activation is sufficient induce HSC division (Nakada et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations cited from prior work.

claim: The selective estrogen receptor modulator tamoxifen promotes HSC division similar to E2.
source: A selective estrogen receptor modulator tamoxifen also promoted HSC division similar to E2 (Sánchez-Aguilera et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: E2 significantly increases HSC divisions but does not lead to HSC depletion, unlike infection or interferon responses.
source: Interestingly, even though E2 significantly increases HSC divisions, unlike infection or interferon responses it does not lead to HSC depletion (Baldridge et al., 2010; Esplin et al., 2011; Essers et al., 2009; Passegué et al., 2005; Sato et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: The unfolded protein response (UPR) is an evolutionally conserved mechanism that promotes protein homeostasis upon various stresses.
source: The unfolded protein response (UPR) is an evolutionally conserved mechanism that promotes protein homeostasis (proteostasis) upon various stresses by increasing the expression of protein foldases and chaperones (Hetz et al., 2013; Janssens et al., 2014; Wang and Kaufman, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: The UPR increases the expression of protein foldases and chaperones.
source: The unfolded protein response (UPR) is an evolutionally conserved mechanism that promotes protein homeostasis (proteostasis) upon various stresses by increasing the expression of protein foldases and chaperones (Hetz et al., 2013; Janssens et al., 2014; Wang and Kaufman, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Three pathways — the PERK-eIF2α-CHOP pathway, the ATF6 pathway, and the IRE1-XBP1 pathway — coordinately regulate the UPR in mammals.
source: Three pathways — the PERK-eIF2α-CHOP pathway, the ATF6 pathway, and the IRE1-XBP1 pathway — coordinately regulate the UPR in mammals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the three branches of the mammalian UPR.

claim: Gpr78 (BiP) is a chaperone localized in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Gpr78 (also called BiP), a chaperone localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), tethers the three ER stress sensors (PERK, ATF6, and IRE1) in inactive states during homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function and localization of Gpr78/BiP.

claim: Gpr78 tethers the three ER stress sensors (PERK, ATF6, and IRE1) in inactive states during homeostasis.
source: Gpr78 (also called BiP), a chaperone localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), tethers the three ER stress sensors (PERK, ATF6, and IRE1) in inactive states during homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of UPR regulation.

claim: Upon ER stress, Gpr78 disassociates with PERK, ATF6, and IRE1 to allow them to become activated and induce the UPR.
source: Upon ER stress, Gpr78 disassociates with PERK, ATF6, and IRE1 to allow them to become activated and induce the UPR.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of UPR activation.

claim: The UPR plays essential roles in highly secretary cells, such as plasma cells and pancreatic β-cells that have high protein flux through the ER.
source: The UPR plays essential roles in highly secretary cells, such as plasma cells and pancreatic β-cells that have high protein flux through the ER.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the importance of UPR in secretory cells.

claim: The UPR is involved in a wide range of pathological states, since many stress signals impinge upon the ER.
source: In addition, recent evidence established that the UPR is also involved in a wide range of pathological states, since many stress signals impinge upon the ER (Malhotra and Kaufman, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: In C. elegans, the UPR can be extrinsically activated, potentially mediated by an as yet unidentified neurotransmitter.
source: Interestingly, evidence in C.elegans indicates that the UPR can be extrinsically activated, potentially mediated by an as yet unidentified neurotransmitter (Sun et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2014; Taylor and Dillin, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: HSCs from E2-treated animals exhibited a greater proportion of immature colonies containing granulocytes, erythrocytes, macrophages, and megakaryocytes (gemM) compared to HSCs from oil-treated mice.
source: HSCs from E2-treated animals exhibited a greater proportion of immature colonies containing granulocytes, erythrocytes, macrophages, and megakaryocytes (gemM) compared to HSCs from oil-treated mice (Figure 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A from colony-forming assays.

claim: E2 increases the multipotency of HSCs.
source: HSCs from E2-treated animals exhibited a greater proportion of immature colonies containing granulocytes, erythrocytes, macrophages, and megakaryocytes (gemM) compared to HSCs from oil-treated mice (Figure 1A), suggesting that E2 increases the multipotency of HSCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the colony-forming assay data showing increased gemM colonies.

claim: Freshly isolated HSCs were incapable of forming any colonies in collagen-based media, potentially due to the lack of HSC supportive cytokines.
source: Although freshly isolated HSCs were incapable of forming any colonies in this media, potentially due to the lack of HSC supportive cytokines, HSCs after a brief culture in media containing cytokines exhibited robust megakaryocytic differentiation in this system.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental protocol with a speculative explanation.

claim: HSCs isolated from E2-treated mice formed more colonies and exhibited a significantly increased capacity to form colonies containing megakaryocytes.
source: We found that HSCs isolated from E2-treated mice not only formed more colonies but they also exhibited a significantly increased capacity to form colonies containing megakaryocytes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B from MegaCult assays.

claim: E2 treatment resulted in significantly more megakaryocytes in the bone marrow compared to oil-treated mice.
source: Consistent with the increased megakaryopoiesis by E2, we observed significantly more megakaryocytes in the bone marrow of E2-treated mice than oil-treated mice (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: E2 treatment enhances the clonogenic potential of HSCs towards myeloid, erythroid, and megakaryocytic lineages.
source: These results indicate that E2 treatment enhances the clonogenic potential of HSCs towards myeloid, erythroid, and megakaryocytic lineages.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results (Figure 1A-D).

claim: HSCs isolated from E2-treated mice exhibited enhanced reconstitution of Mac-1/Gr-1+ myeloid cells, Ter119+ red blood cells, and CD41+ platelets compared to oil-treated controls.
source: Compared to oil-treated controls, HSCs isolated from E2-treated mice exhibited enhanced reconstitution of Mac-1/Gr-1+ myeloid cells, Ter119+ red blood cells, and CD41+ platelets (Figure 1E–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive transplantation data shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: HSCs from E2-treated mice did not exhibit reduced lymphoid cell reconstitution.
source: Interestingly, HSCs from E2-treated mice did not exhibit reduced lymphoid cell reconstitution (Figure 1I–J), indicating that the enhanced myeloid/erythroid/megakaryocytic cell reconstitution by E2 stimulated HSCs was not at the cost of lymphoid cell reconstitution.
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 1I-J.

claim: The enhanced myeloid/erythroid/megakaryocytic cell reconstitution by E2 stimulated HSCs was not at the cost of lymphoid cell reconstitution.
source: Interestingly, HSCs from E2-treated mice did not exhibit reduced lymphoid cell reconstitution (Figure 1I–J), indicating that the enhanced myeloid/erythroid/megakaryocytic cell reconstitution by E2 stimulated HSCs was not at the cost of lymphoid cell reconstitution.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that lymphoid reconstitution was maintained.

claim: Reconstituted bone marrow derived from E2-treated HSCs gave rise to stable engraftment across all lineages in secondary recipients.
source: Reconstituted bone marrow derived from E2-treated HSCs gave rise to stable engraftment across all lineages in secondary recipients (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by secondary transplantation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Although E2 treatment increases HSC division, it does not negatively affect long-term self-renewal capacity of HSCs but rather increases HSC function.
source: Therefore, although E2 treatment increases HSC division (Nakada et al., 2014), it does not negatively affect long-term self-renewal capacity of HSCs but rather increases HSC function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transplantation data combined with prior knowledge about E2 effects on HSC division.

claim: The increased ability of E2-stimulated HSCs to form immature colonies and megakaryocytes was abolished by deleting ERα.
source: The increased ability of E2-stimulated HSCs to form immature colonies (Figure 1A) and megakaryocytes (Figure 1B) was abolished by deleting ERα, indicating that ERα promotes HSC function upon E2 stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from ERα-deficient mice shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: ERα promotes HSC function upon E2 stimulation.
source: The increased ability of E2-stimulated HSCs to form immature colonies (Figure 1A) and megakaryocytes (Figure 1B) was abolished by deleting ERα, indicating that ERα promotes HSC function upon E2 stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the loss of E2 effects in ERα-deficient mice.

claim: ERα-deficient HSCs without E2 stimulation exhibited intact long-term multilineage reconstitution.
source: ERα-deficient HSCs without E2 stimulation exhibited intact long-term multilineage reconstitution (Figure 1E–J), indicating that ERα is dispensable for steady state HSC function, as shown previously (Thurmond et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation data from ERα-deficient mice shown in Figure 1E-J.

claim: ERα is dispensable for steady state HSC function.
source: ERα-deficient HSCs without E2 stimulation exhibited intact long-term multilineage reconstitution (Figure 1E–J), indicating that ERα is dispensable for steady state HSC function, as shown previously (Thurmond et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the normal function of ERα-deficient HSCs without E2 treatment, supported by a citation.

claim: ERα-deficient HSCs did not exhibit increased myeloid/erythroid/megakaryocytic cell reconstitution upon E2 treatment.
source: However, ERα-deficient HSCs did not exhibit increased myeloid/erythroid/megakaryocytic cell reconstitution upon E2 treatment as observed in wild-type HSCs (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation data from ERα-deficient mice shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: The E2-ERα pathway enhances functions within the hematopoietic cells to promote myeloid/erythroid/megakaryocytic reconstitution by HSCs in response to E2.
source: These results establish that the E2-ERα pathway enhances functions within the hematopoietic cells to promote myeloid/erythroid/megakaryocytic reconstitution by HSCs in response to E2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ERα deletion experiments showing cell-autonomous effects.

claim: E2 treatment prior to irradiation significantly accelerated the rate at which platelets and white blood cells recover.
source: Serial sampling of peripheral blood after irradiation revealed that E2 treatment prior to irradiation significantly accelerated the rate at which platelets and white blood cells recover, whereas the effects on red blood cell counts were modest (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by peripheral blood count data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: E2 treatment prior to irradiation had modest effects on red blood cell recovery.
source: Serial sampling of peripheral blood after irradiation revealed that E2 treatment prior to irradiation significantly accelerated the rate at which platelets and white blood cells recover, whereas the effects on red blood cell counts were modest (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by peripheral blood count data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The accelerated recovery of RBC, PLT, and WBC in E2-treated mice was not observed in ERα-deficient mice.
source: The accelerated recovery of RBC, PLT, and WBC in E2-treated mice was not observed in ERα-deficient mice, indicating that ERα is required for E2 to promote regeneration (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from ERα-deficient mice shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: ERα is required for E2 to promote hematopoietic regeneration after irradiation.
source: The accelerated recovery of RBC, PLT, and WBC in E2-treated mice was not observed in ERα-deficient mice, indicating that ERα is required for E2 to promote regeneration (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the loss of E2 effects in ERα-deficient mice.

claim: E2 treatment promotes hematopoietic recovery after stress.
source: These results indicate that E2 treatment promotes hematopoietic recovery after stress, consistent with our prior finding that E2 promotes the reconstitution potential of HSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the irradiation recovery data.

claim: 89% of oil-treated male mice died within 28 days after 800 cGy irradiation.
source: Whereas 89% of oil-treated mice died within 28 days after irradiation, E2 treatment significantly reduced the fraction (to 29%) of mice succumbing to irradiation-induced lethality (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: E2 treatment significantly reduced the fraction of mice succumbing to irradiation-induced lethality to 29%.
source: Whereas 89% of oil-treated mice died within 28 days after irradiation, E2 treatment significantly reduced the fraction (to 29%) of mice succumbing to irradiation-induced lethality (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Female mice are more radioresistant than male mice.
source: This increased survival is consistent with an early study that described that female mice are more radioresistant than male mice, which we confirmed here (Figure 2H), and that the estrus cycle affects the radiosensitivity of female mice (Rugh and Clugston, 1955).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2H and a citation to prior work.

claim: The estrus cycle affects the radiosensitivity of female mice.
source: This increased survival is consistent with an early study that described that female mice are more radioresistant than male mice, which we confirmed here (Figure 2H), and that the estrus cycle affects the radiosensitivity of female mice (Rugh and Clugston, 1955).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The positive effect of E2 on hematopoietic regeneration improves the survival of mice after hematopoietic injury.
source: These results suggest that the positive effect of E2 on hematopoietic regeneration improves the survival of mice after hematopoietic injury.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the survival data after irradiation.

claim: E2 treatment significantly accelerated the recovery of whole bone marrow cells at days 5, 7, and 14 after irradiation.
source: E2 treatment significantly accelerated the recovery of whole bone marrow (WBM) cells at days 5, 7, and 14 after irradiation (Figure 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by bone marrow cellularity data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Irradiation caused rapid and prolonged depletion of immature lineage-Sca-1+c-kit+ (LSK) cells for up to two weeks post irradiation.
source: Irradiation caused rapid and prolonged depletion of immature lineage-Sca-1+c-kit+ (LSK) cells for up to two weeks post irradiation (0.17 ± 0.04% before irradiation versus 0.02 ± 0.02% at two weeks after irradiation).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring LSK cell frequencies.

claim: E2 treatment prior to irradiation significantly increased the frequency of LSK cells compared to control oil-treated mice 14 days after TBI.
source: Intriguingly, E2 treatment prior to irradiation significantly increased the frequency of LSK cells compared to control oil-treated mice 14 days after TBI (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: E2 treatment induced a 6.3-fold expansion of the LSK pool at day 14 after irradiation.
source: Combined with the increased numbers of WBM cells in E2-treated irradiated mice, E2 treatment induced a 6.3-fold expansion (p<0.01) of the size of LSK pool at day 14 (Figure 3C)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of LSK cell numbers shown in Figure 3C.

claim: E2 treatment prior to TBI promotes LSK regeneration.
source: Combined with the increased numbers of WBM cells in E2-treated irradiated mice, E2 treatment induced a 6.3-fold expansion (p<0.01) of the size of LSK pool at day 14 (Figure 3C), suggesting that E2 treatment prior to TBI promotes LSK regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the increased LSK cell numbers after E2 treatment.

claim: E2 treatments every other day post-TBI increased hematopoietic cell numbers after irradiation.
source: E2 treatments every other day post-TBI also increased hematopoietic cell numbers after irradiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: E2 treatment did not significantly affect the frequency of lineage-Sca-1-c-kit+ committed myeloid progenitors (MP), but did increase the total numbers of these cells.
source: In contrast, E2 treatment did not significantly affect the frequency of lineage-Sca-1-c-kit+ committed myeloid progenitors (MP), but did increase the total numbers of these cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-H.

claim: E2 treatment resulted in significantly lower numbers of Annexin V+ lineage- BM cells at both days 3 and 5 post-TBI.
source: We assessed apoptosis rates in lineage- BM cells shortly after irradiation exposure by Annexin V staining and observed significantly lower numbers of Annexin V+ cells in E2 treated cohorts at both days 3 and 5 post-TBI (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The preservation of HSPC numbers by E2 treatment could be a function of enhanced proliferation, protection from irradiation-induced apoptosis, or a combination of both.
source: These results suggest that the preservation of HSPC numbers by E2 treatment could be a function of enhanced proliferation (Nakada et al., 2014), protection from irradiation-induced apoptosis, or a combination of both.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data combining observations about proliferation and apoptosis.

claim: E2 not only enhances recuperation of peripheral blood cells after irradiation but also enhances hematopoietic regeneration by promoting the recovery of immature HSPCs.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that E2 not only enhances recuperation of peripheral blood cells after irradiation (Figure 2A–C), but also enhances hematopoietic regeneration by promoting the recovery of immature HSPCs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: Irradiation compromised the expression of several HSC markers.
source: Since irradiation compromised the expression of several HSC markers (data not shown and (Simonnet et al., 2009), we accessed long-term reconstitution capacity as a surrogate of HSC function by transplanting WBM cells from irradiated animals that had been treated with control oil or E2 into wild-type recipients.
evidence: This statement is supported by unpublished data and a citation to prior work.

claim: Cells from irradiated, oil-treated mice exhibited negligible reconstitution upon transplantation.
source: Cells from irradiated, oil-treated mice exhibited negligible reconstitution upon transplantation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cells from mice that were treated with E2 prior to irradiation demonstrated a preservation of long-term reconstitution potential in the myeloid, erythroid, and platelet lineages.
source: Strikingly, we observed that cells from mice that were treated with E2 prior to irradiation demonstrated a preservation of long-term reconstitution potential in the myeloid, erythroid, and platelet lineages — a feature that reflects HSC activity (Oguro et al., 2013; Pietras et al., 2015; Sanjuan-Pla et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2013) — although their lymphoid-reconstitution potential was impaired.
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 3D and citations to prior work defining HSC activity.

claim: Long-term myeloid reconstitution capacity is a feature that reflects HSC activity.
source: Strikingly, we observed that cells from mice that were treated with E2 prior to irradiation demonstrated a preservation of long-term reconstitution potential in the myeloid, erythroid, and platelet lineages — a feature that reflects HSC activity (Oguro et al., 2013; Pietras et al., 2015; Sanjuan-Pla et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2013) — although their lymphoid-reconstitution potential was impaired.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Lymphoid-reconstitution potential was impaired in cells from E2-treated irradiated mice.
source: Strikingly, we observed that cells from mice that were treated with E2 prior to irradiation demonstrated a preservation of long-term reconstitution potential in the myeloid, erythroid, and platelet lineages — a feature that reflects HSC activity (Oguro et al., 2013; Pietras et al., 2015; Sanjuan-Pla et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2013) — although their lymphoid-reconstitution potential was impaired.
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: E2 treatment improves the regeneration of the hematopoietic system, augmenting the function of cells with long-term myeloid reconstitution capacity.
source: These results demonstrate that E2 treatment improves the regeneration of the hematopoietic system, augmenting the function of cells with long-term myeloid reconstitution capacity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transplantation data.

claim: Deleting ERα abolished the accelerated recovery of bone marrow cellularity after irradiation in response to prior E2 treatment.
source: We found that deleting ERα abolished the accelerated recovery of bone marrow cellularity after irradiation in response to prior E2 treatment (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from ERα-deficient mice shown in Figure 3E.

claim: E2 treatment promoted the regeneration of LSK cells in the bone marrow after irradiation, but failed to do so in ERα-deficient mice.
source: Furthermore, whereas E2 treatment promoted the regeneration of LSK cells in the bone marrow after irradiation, it failed to do so in ERα-deficient mice (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from ERα-deficient mice shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: ERα, which is highly expressed in HSPCs, promotes hematopoietic regeneration in response to E2 stimulation.
source: These results indicate that ERα, which is highly expressed in HSPCs, promotes hematopoietic regeneration in response to E2 stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ERα deletion experiments, with the expression level being established knowledge.

claim: Wild-type HSCs from E2-treated mice clustered separately from other groups in unsupervised hierarchical clustering analysis.
source: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering analysis revealed that wild-type HSCs from E2-treated mice clustered separately from other groups, indicating that E2 induces a transcriptional response that is dependent on ERα (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: E2 induces a transcriptional response in HSCs that is dependent on ERα.
source: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering analysis revealed that wild-type HSCs from E2-treated mice clustered separately from other groups, indicating that E2 induces a transcriptional response that is dependent on ERα (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clustering analysis showing distinct transcriptional profiles.

claim: Myc and E2F target genes and genes involved in cell cycle regulation were enriched in E2-treated HSCs.
source: The GSEA revealed that Myc and E2F target genes and genes involved in cell cycle regulation were enriched in E2-treated HSCs (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–H)
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Several Myc target genes were induced by E2 treatment in vitro.
source: Several Myc target genes were induced by E2 treatment in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–H), although c-Myc, N-Myc, and L-Myc were not induced in HSCs by E2 as determined by RNA-seq (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-H.

claim: c-Myc, N-Myc, and L-Myc were not induced in HSCs by E2 as determined by RNA-seq.
source: Several Myc target genes were induced by E2 treatment in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–H), although c-Myc, N-Myc, and L-Myc were not induced in HSCs by E2 as determined by RNA-seq (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished RNA-seq data.

claim: Several megakaryocyte lineage genes were increased in E2 treated HSCs.
source: Additionally, several megakaryocyte lineage genes were increased in E2 treated HSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: A gene set representing the unfolded protein response (UPR) was upregulated in HSCs in response to E2.
source: Interestingly, we found that a gene set representing the unfolded protein response (UPR) was also upregulated in HSCs in response to E2 (Figure 4B Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Wild-type HSCs from E2-treated mice have significant enrichment of UPR related genes compared to all other treatment groups, including E2-treated ERα-deficient HSCs.
source: We found that wild-type HSCs from E2-treated mice have significant (p<0.005) enrichment of UPR related genes compared to all other treatment groups, including E2-treated ERα-deficient HSCs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by pairwise GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: E2 treatment induces the UPR in HSCs in an ERα-dependent manner.
source: This analysis indicates that E2 treatment induces the UPR in HSCs in an ERα-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GSEA analysis showing ERα-dependent UPR gene enrichment.

claim: The expression of Ern1, which encodes Ire1α, was significantly increased in E2-treated HSCs.
source: Importantly, we found that the expression of Ern1, which encodes a key regulator of the UPR, Ire1α, was significantly increased in E2-treated HSCs (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A and D.

claim: The increased expression of Ern1 was evident in previously published microarray analysis (GDS4944).
source: The increased expression of Ern1 was also evident in our previously published microarray analysis (GDS4944) (Nakada et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement references prior published data from the authors.

claim: Multiple chaperones were induced in HSCs by E2.
source: Moreover, multiple chaperones were induced in HSCs by E2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: The UPR was increased in HSCs after E2 exposure.
source: These results suggested that the UPR was increased in HSCs after E2 exposure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including RNA-seq and gene expression data.

claim: The induction of Ern1 in HSCs upon E2 treatment was fully dependent on ERα.
source: Consistent with our RNA-seq analysis, we confirmed that the induction of Ern1 in HSCs upon E2 treatment was fully dependent on ERα (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The components of the two other UPR branches, such as Ddit3 (encoding CHOP), Eifak3 (encoding PERK), and Atf6, were unaffected by E2 treatment.
source: However, the components of the two other UPR branches, such as Ddit3 (encoding CHOP), Eifak3 (encoding PERK), and, Atf6, were unaffected by E2 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that the Ire1α pathway is activated upon E2 stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The Ire1α pathway is activated upon E2 stimulation.
source: However, the components of the two other UPR branches, such as Ddit3 (encoding CHOP), Eifak3 (encoding PERK), and, Atf6, were unaffected by E2 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that the Ire1α pathway is activated upon E2 stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the selective induction of Ire1α without changes in other UPR branches.

claim: Ire1α levels were increased consistently across CD150-defined subsets of CD48-/low LSK cells.
source: To test whether Ire1α was activated in a lineage-biased subset of HSCs we examined Ire1α expression in CD48-/low LSK cells fractionated based on CD150 expression levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B) (Beerman et al., 2010). Ire1α levels were increased consistently across each subset indicating that E2 acts on the entirety of the HSC pool.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: E2 acts on the entirety of the HSC pool.
source: Ire1α levels were increased consistently across each subset indicating that E2 acts on the entirety of the HSC pool.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the uniform induction of Ire1α across HSC subsets.

claim: Ire1α is a bifunctional protein with a serine-threonine kinase domain and an RNase domain.
source: Ire1α is a bifunctional protein with a serine-threonine kinase domain and an RNase domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of Ire1α.

claim: In response to ER stress, the RNase activity of Ire1α becomes activated and splices Xbp1 mRNA.
source: In response to ER stress, the RNase activity of Ire1α becomes activated and splices Xbp1 mRNA (Cox and Walter, 1996; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Xbp1 splicing produces a functional Xbp1s protein that serves as a transcriptional regulator critical for the induction of UPR response genes.
source: This Xbp1 splicing event produces a functional Xbp1s protein that serves as a transcriptional regulator critical for the induction of UPR response genes (Hetz et al., 2013; Janssens et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Xbp1 splicing was induced in response to E2 treatment in both HSCs and MPPs, but not in WBM cells.
source: We found that Xbp1 splicing was induced in response to E2 treatment in both HSCs and MPPs, but not in WBM cells, suggesting that immature hematopoietic progenitor cells are more sensitive to E2 treatment to activate Xbp1 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Immature hematopoietic progenitor cells are more sensitive to E2 treatment to activate Xbp1.
source: We found that Xbp1 splicing was induced in response to E2 treatment in both HSCs and MPPs, but not in WBM cells, suggesting that immature hematopoietic progenitor cells are more sensitive to E2 treatment to activate Xbp1 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential Xbp1 splicing in different cell types.

claim: Xbp1 splicing, as determined by Venus fluorescence in ERAI mice, was significantly increased by E2 treatment in HSCs and MPPs, but not in lineage- and WBM cells.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of cells isolated from ERAI mice treated with oil or E2 revealed that Xbp1 splicing, as determined by Venus fluorescence, was significantly increased by E2 treatment in HSCs and MPPs, but not in lineage- and WBM cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data from ERAI mice shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Xbp1 splicing was entirely dependent upon ERα.
source: Importantly, Xbp1 splicing was entirely dependent upon ERα, consistent with our finding that the E2-ERα pathway induces Ire1α expression (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from ERα-deficient mice shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The protein levels of Ire1α and Xbp1s were increased upon E2 treatment in both CD48-/low and CD48+ fractions of the LSK population, but not in WBM cells.
source: We also confirmed that the protein levels of Ire1α and Xbp1s were increased upon E2 treatment in both CD48-/low (containing HSCs and MPPs) and CD48+ fractions of the LSK population, but not in WBM cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The Ire1α-Xbp1 branch of the UPR is activated in E2-treated HSCs.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the Ire1α-Xbp1 branch of the UPR is activated in E2-treated HSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including gene expression, protein levels, and Xbp1 splicing data.

claim: HSCs and MPPs had significantly lower protein translation compared to whole bone marrow cells.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Signer et al., 2014), HSCs and MPPs had significantly lower protein translation compared to whole bone marrow cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by puromycin incorporation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and a citation.

claim: The protein synthesis rate of HSCs did not significantly change upon E2 treatment.
source: However, the protein synthesis rate of HSCs did not significantly change upon E2 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), consistent with a previous report demonstrating that cycling HSCs do not have increased protein translation (Signer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by puromycin incorporation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and a citation.

claim: Inducing HSCs to proliferate by G-CSF or poly I:C administration did not increase Ire1α expression.
source: Moreover, inducing HSCs to proliferate (either by G-CSF or poly I:C administration) did not increase Ire1α expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: G-CSF or poly I:C treatment had limited effects on the expression of chaperone genes compared to E2.
source: and these treatment had limited effects on the expression of chaperone genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G) compared to the broad effects E2 had on chaperones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G and 1K.

claim: Activation of the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway is not a general response used by HSCs upon cell cycle activation.
source: Thus, activation of the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway is not a general response used by HSCs upon cell cycle activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of Ire1α induction in HSCs activated by other stimuli.

claim: Both the de novo and the supervised motif search identified ERE as the most enriched motif found in differentially regulated ATAC-seq peaks.
source: Both the de novo and the supervised motif search identified ERE as the most enriched motif found in differentially regulated peaks, consistent with the idea that ERα is the major regulator of the transcriptional changes induced by E2 in HSCs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq motif analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ERα is the major regulator of the transcriptional changes induced by E2 in HSCs.
source: Both the de novo and the supervised motif search identified ERE as the most enriched motif found in differentially regulated peaks, consistent with the idea that ERα is the major regulator of the transcriptional changes induced by E2 in HSCs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of ERE motifs in E2-responsive chromatin regions.

claim: One of the differential ATAC-seq peaks present in E2-treated HSCs was located approximately 2.5 kb upstream of the TSS of Ire1α.
source: Of interest, one of the differential peaks present in E2-treated HSCs was located approximately 2.5 kb upstream of the TSS of Ire1α (termed peak 2) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ATAC-seq peak upstream of Ire1α contains a ERE motif with one nucleotide mismatch from the consensus ERE.
source: Further sequence interrogation of this locus revealed that this ATAC-seq peak contains a ERE motif with one nucleotide mismatch (GGTCAnnnTGACa) from the consensus ERE (Figure 5C, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis of the ATAC-seq peak shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ERE motifs found in prototypical ERα target genes, such as Oxytocin and pS2, contain one base mismatch from the consensus.
source: Given that ERE motifs found in prototypical ERα target genes, such as Oxytocin and pS2, contain one base mismatch from the consensus (Gruber et al., 2004), we next functionally validated the ERE in this locus.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The Ern1(-4 kb) construct has E2- and ERα-responsive transactivating capacity.
source: This revealed that the Ern1(−4 kb) construct has E2- and ERα-responsive transactivating capacity (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The E2- and ERα-responsive transactivating capacity of the Ern1(-4 kb) construct was diminished when the ERE was mutated.
source: Importantly, this E2- and ERα-responsive transactivating capacity was diminished when the ERE was mutated in the Ern1(−4 kb) construct, indicating that the ERE located upstream of Ern1 is functional.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data with mutated ERE shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The ERE located upstream of Ern1 is functional.
source: Importantly, this E2- and ERα-responsive transactivating capacity was diminished when the ERE was mutated in the Ern1(−4 kb) construct, indicating that the ERE located upstream of Ern1 is functional.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the loss of transactivation when the ERE is mutated.

claim: ERα occupancy at peak 2 upstream of Ire1α increased significantly upon E2 treatment in c-kit+ HSPCs.
source: We found that the ERα occupancy at peak 2 increased significantly upon E2 treatment (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ire1α is a direct target of ligand-activated ERα in hematopoietic progenitor cells.
source: These results establish that Ire1α is a direct target of ligand-activated ERα in hematopoietic progenitor cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including ATAC-seq, luciferase assays, and ChIP-qPCR.

claim: Both tunicamycin and thapsigargin increased the frequencies of Annexin V+ LSK cells.
source: Both tunicamycin and thapsigargin increased the frequencies of Annexin V+ LSK cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B) and reduced clonogenicity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Tunicamycin and thapsigargin reduced clonogenicity of LSK cells.
source: Both tunicamycin and thapsigargin increased the frequencies of Annexin V+ LSK cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B) and reduced clonogenicity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In vivo E2 treatment significantly rescued the effects of ER stressors on LSK cell viability and clonogenicity.
source: However, in vivo E2 treatment significantly rescued these effects, indicating that HSPCs exposed to E2 are protected from proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: HSPCs exposed to E2 are protected from proteotoxic stress.
source: However, in vivo E2 treatment significantly rescued these effects, indicating that HSPCs exposed to E2 are protected from proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rescue of ER stress effects by E2 treatment.

claim: The E2-ERα pathway confers resistance against ER stress.
source: These results establish that the E2-ERα pathway confers resistance against ER stress, paralleling the activation of the protective Ire1α-Xbp1 branch of the UPR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ER stress resistance data.

claim: Increased oxidative stress can cause protein oxidation, leading to accumulation of protein aggregates, which in turn elicits ER stress and activates the UPR.
source: Increased oxidative stress, such as that caused by ionizing irradiation, can cause protein oxidation, leading to accumulation of protein aggregates, which in turn elicits ER stress and activates the UPR (Berlett and Stadtman, 1997; Malhotra and Kaufman, 2007; Squier, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: A dose-dependent increase in the levels of protein aggregates was observed following sublethal doses of irradiation.
source: We quantified protein aggregates using a recently published protocol (Sigurdsson et al., 2016), and observed a dose-dependent increase in the levels of protein aggregates following sublethal doses of irradiation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Proteostat staining data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: E2-treatment significantly reduced the levels of protein aggregates after TBI in LSK cells but not WBM cells.
source: Interestingly, E2-treatment significantly reduced the levels of protein aggregates after TBI in LSK cells but not WBM cells, in concordance with the induction of Ire1α and splicing of Xbp1 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Proteostat staining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Deleting Ire1α abolished the resistance endowed by E2 against ER stressors.
source: Strikingly, we found that deleting Ire1α abolished the resistance endowed by E2 against ER stressors (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony assay data from CRISPR-edited cells shown in Figure 6D.

claim: E2 promotes ER stress resistance by activating the cytoprotective UPR branch governed by the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway.
source: These results demonstrate that E2 promotes ER stress resistance by activating the cytoprotective UPR branch governed by the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CRISPR deletion experiments showing Ire1α is required for E2-mediated stress resistance.

claim: Recipients of Rosa26-edited LSK cells demonstrated enhanced hematopoietic recovery when treated with E2, which was largely suppressed when Ire1α was deleted.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Figure 2D–F), recipients of Rosa26-edited LSK cells demonstrated enhanced hematopoietic recovery when treated with E2, which was largely suppressed when Ire1α was deleted (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by peripheral blood count data from transplant recipients shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The frequencies of LSK and myeloid progenitor cells were significantly increased in mice receiving E2 treatment after transplantation.
source: The frequencies of LSK and myeloid progenitor cells were significantly increased in mice receiving E2 treatment after transplantation (Figure 6F–G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: The effect of E2 on LSK and myeloid progenitor regeneration was abolished in recipients of Ire1α-edited LSK cells.
source: However, this effect was abolished in similarly treated recipients of Ire1α-edited LSK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: The E2-ERα module activates and at least partly depends on the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway to promote hematopoietic regeneration.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that the E2-ERα module activates and at least partly depends on the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway to promote hematopoietic regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the CRISPR deletion experiments in transplantation.

claim: Whether activation of the UPR is beneficial or detrimental for HSC function depends on which pathway becomes activated and to what extent it is activated.
source: Whether activation of the UPR is beneficial or detrimental for HSC function appears to depend on which pathway becomes activated and to what extent it is activated.
evidence: This is a general statement synthesizing knowledge from the field.

claim: Deletion of Grp78 (BiP) in mice activates all three branches of the UPR and reduces the HSC pool, causing lymphopenia.
source: Deletion of Grp78 (BiP) in mice activates all three branches of the UPR and reduces the HSC pool, causing lymphopenia (Wey et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Human HSCs activate the PERK pathway upon proteotoxic stress, rendering them susceptible to apoptosis.
source: Human HSCs activate the PERK pathway upon proteotoxic stress, rendering them susceptible to apoptosis (van Galen et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: While human HSCs activate the PERK pathway upon proteotoxic stress and undergo apoptosis, downstream progenitors activate the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway to survive.
source: While human HSCs activate the PERK pathway upon proteotoxic stress and undergo apoptosis, downstream progenitors activate the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway to survive (van Galen et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Overexpression of a molecular chaperone ERDJ4 (encoded by DNAJB9) protects human HSCs from proteotoxic stress and increases the reconstitution capacity.
source: Additionally, overexpression of a molecular chaperone ERDJ4 (encoded by DNAJB9) protects human HSCs from proteotoxic stress and increases the reconstitution capacity (van Galen et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Activation of the Ire1α-Xbp1 branch by E2 protects HSCs from proteotoxic stress and promotes hematopoietic regeneration.
source: Our results are consistent with the model that activation of the Ire1α-Xbp1 branch by E2 protects HSCs from proteotoxic stress and promotes hematopoietic regeneration, although we cannot formally exclude the possibility that two other UPR branches (PERK and ATF6) are also involved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with a caveat about other pathways.

claim: RIDD seems unlikely to be activated in E2-treated HSCs since translation is not attenuated in HSCs after E2 exposure.
source: However, RIDD seems unlikely to be activated in E2-treated HSCs since translation is not attenuated in HSCs after E2 exposure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of translation attenuation, which is typically associated with RIDD.

claim: RIDD is usually associated with apoptotic cell death, which is not observed in E2-treated cells.
source: Furthermore, RIDD is usually associated with apoptotic cell death, which is not observed in E2-treated cells.
evidence: This statement combines established knowledge about RIDD with observations from the current study.

claim: Xbp1 is largely dispensable for HSC maintenance during homeostasis.
source: It is important to note that Xbp1 is largely dispensable for HSC maintenance during homeostasis (Bettigole et al., 2015), indicating that although Xbp1 is not required for the homeostatic maintenance of HSCs, its activation provides additional protection against proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Although Xbp1 is not required for the homeostatic maintenance of HSCs, its activation provides additional protection against proteotoxic stress.
source: It is important to note that Xbp1 is largely dispensable for HSC maintenance during homeostasis (Bettigole et al., 2015), indicating that although Xbp1 is not required for the homeostatic maintenance of HSCs, its activation provides additional protection against proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dispensability of Xbp1 during homeostasis combined with its protective effects during stress.

claim: Selective activation of the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway is key to harnessing the UPR to improve hematopoietic regeneration.
source: Thus, selective activation of the Ire1α-Xbp1 pathway is key to harnessing the UPR to improve hematopoietic regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of UPR branches on HSC function.

claim: E2-treated HSCs had increased expression of genes known as Myc target genes, some of which were induced in vitro after E2 stimulation.
source: Consistent with our previous finding that E2 promotes division of HSCs (Nakada et al., 2014), we found that E2-treated HSCs had increased expression of genes known as Myc target genes, some of which were induced in vitro after E2 stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and in vitro qPCR data.

claim: Female mice are more resistant to acute irradiation than male mice.
source: An earlier study reported that female mice are more resistant to acute irradiation than male mice, and that the estrus cycle affects radioresistance (Rugh and Clugston, 1955), although careful interpretation is required since strain differences also contribute to radioresistance (Grahn, 1958).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Strain differences contribute to radioresistance in mice.
source: An earlier study reported that female mice are more resistant to acute irradiation than male mice, and that the estrus cycle affects radioresistance (Rugh and Clugston, 1955), although careful interpretation is required since strain differences also contribute to radioresistance (Grahn, 1958).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Estrogenic compounds such as genistein have radioprotective effects.
source: Estrogenic compounds such as genistein have also been known to have radioprotective effects (Ha et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Engraftment of human HSPCs is more efficient in female recipient mice than male mice.
source: Additionally, it has been demonstrated that engraftment of human HSPCs is more efficient in female recipient mice than male mice (Notta et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The female hormonal milieu may protect engrafting HSCs from stress.
source: The mechanism behind this sexual difference in HSC engraftment remains to be established, but it is tempting to speculate that the female hormonal milieu protects engrafting HSCs from stress.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Estrogens have detrimental hematopoietic side-effects, such as causing thromboembolism.
source: Since estrogens also have detrimental hematopoietic side-effects, such as causing thromboembolism (Tchaikovski and Rosing, 2010), future studies should aim to separate the beneficial effects of estrogens on HSC function from other negative effects.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The effects of E2 on mature cells in the blood were less pronounced than the effects on HSPCs.
source: In concordance with the effect of E2 on HSPC regeneration, E2 also improved the blood cell counts after irradiation or transplantation, although the effects of E2 on mature cells in the blood were less pronounced than the effects on HSPCs.
evidence: This is an observation comparing the magnitude of effects on different cell populations.

claim: Production of mature blood cells involves multiple intermediate cell stages during differentiation and is affected by a variety of homeostatic mechanisms.
source: We postulate that since production of mature cells involves multiple intermediate cell stages during differentiation and that it is also affected by a variety of homeostatic mechanisms (such as thrombopoietin production by the liver and the kidney), the end output in the blood may not be as robust as the effects on HSPCs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the differential effects on HSPCs versus mature cells.

claim: Chemical chaperones aid in cellular protein folding capacity to maintain proteostasis, and have therapeutic potential in treating metabolic and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Chemical chaperones, such as osmolytes and hydrophobic compounds, aid in cellular protein folding capacity to maintain proteostasis, and have therapeutic potential in treating metabolic and neurodegenerative diseases (Cortez and Sim, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Taurocholic acid is more abundant in the bile acid of fetal liver compared to adult liver.
source: Interestingly, taurocholic acid, a chemical chaperone that is more abundant in the bile acid of fetal liver compared to adult liver, inhibits protein aggregation in fetal liver HSCs to support their rapid expansion during development and in culture (Miharada et al., 2014; Sigurdsson et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Taurocholic acid inhibits protein aggregation in fetal liver HSCs to support their rapid expansion during development and in culture.
source: Interestingly, taurocholic acid, a chemical chaperone that is more abundant in the bile acid of fetal liver compared to adult liver, inhibits protein aggregation in fetal liver HSCs to support their rapid expansion during development and in culture (Miharada et al., 2014; Sigurdsson et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Systemic factors can affect the protein folding capacity of HSCs.
source: This illustrates that systemic factor(s) can affect the protein folding capacity of HSCs, although it remains unclear whether bile acid affects the UPR of HSCs in adult animals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the taurocholic acid example.

claim: It remains unclear whether bile acid affects the UPR of HSCs in adult animals.
source: This illustrates that systemic factor(s) can affect the protein folding capacity of HSCs, although it remains unclear whether bile acid affects the UPR of HSCs in adult animals.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: In nematodes and fruit flies, impaired proteostasis of a cell type or a tissue can communicate to other cells to coordinate stress responses systemically by upregulating the UPR in the periphery.
source: In nematodes and fruit flies, impaired proteostasis of a cell type or a tissue can communicate to other cells to coordinate stress responses systemically by upregulating the UPR in the periphery (Berendzen et al., 2016; van Oosten-Hawle and Morimoto, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Activation of the UPR in neurons by Xbp1s expression extends lifespan of C. elegans.
source: Additionally, activation of the UPR in neurons by Xbp1s expression extends lifespan of C.elegans, and strikingly, augments the UPR in the intestine through a cell non-autonomous mechanism involving an unknown neurotransmitter (Taylor and Dillin, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Neuronal Xbp1s expression augments the UPR in the intestine of C. elegans through a cell non-autonomous mechanism involving an unknown neurotransmitter.
source: Additionally, activation of the UPR in neurons by Xbp1s expression extends lifespan of C.elegans, and strikingly, augments the UPR in the intestine through a cell non-autonomous mechanism involving an unknown neurotransmitter (Taylor and Dillin, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The Ire1α-Xbp1s pathway is important for systemic UPR activation in vertebrates.

claim: The UPR is a conserved mechanism that is activated by systemic factors to prepare the perceiving cells against stress by promoting proteostasis.
source: Thus, although the secreted systemic factors that activate the UPR in distal tissues remain largely unknown, the UPR is a conserved mechanism that is activated by systemic factors to prepare the perceiving cells against stress by promoting proteostasis.
